A TRUE HERO FINALLY RETURNS HOME

In a moment of unimaginable terror, a 12-year-old girl displayed the kind of selfless bravery that defines true heroes, stepping directly in front of danger and taking three bullets to protect her classmates.

What followed was a grueling 262-day fight for survival inside the hospital, marked by numerous surgeries, intensive rehabilitation, and an unbreakable spirit.

Now, after nearly nine months of fighting every single day, she has finally walked out of the hospital and returned home to her family, friends, and community.

Her courage saved lives, and her resilience through nearly 300 days of medical battles serves as an inspiring reminder of the power of the human spirit.

Drop a prayer and show your respect for this brave 12-year-old warrior in the comments below.

Sound off with your messages of support, let’s welcome this hero home.

As national discussions continue over the future of the Pentagon, Pete Hegseth's platform to overhaul defense leadership continues to draw passionate grassroots backing nationwide.

With an emphasis on rebuilding combat readiness, cutting bureaucratic overhead, and returning the armed services to pure warfighting standards, supporters view his leadership as a vital shift in military culture.

🚨BREAKING NEWS 🚨 A devastating crash in North Hollywood has left at least three people dead and three others fighting for their lives in critical condition after a vehicle plowed into a crowded sidewalk food stand on Tuesday night.

Emergency crews rushed to the intersection of Lankershim and Chandler Boulevard near a busy Metro transit station, where the out-of-control vehicle slammed through a taco stand, scattering debris across the sidewalk and trapping pedestrians.

Prayers go out to the victims, the injured, and their families tonight as investigators work to determine what caused this tragedy.

A newly unsealed Department of Defense investigation has revealed an alarming national security crisis off the coast of Southern California, where millions of gallons of raw, untreated sewage flowing across the border from Mexico are routinely sickening America's elite Navy SEAL trainees.

According to a scathing Pentagon Inspector General report, Navy SEAL and Special Warfare Combat Crewman candidates conducting grueling ocean training off Naval Amphibious Base Coronado are repeatedly exposed to dangerous levels of waterborne bacteria and fecal runoff from the Tijuana River. Between 2019 and 2023, military doctors diagnosed nearly 1,200 cases of severe acute gastrointestinal illness among trainees who were forced to swim in waters that local authorities had already closed to the public.

The pollution crisis has grown so severe that Naval Special Warfare Command has repeatedly been forced to halt training in Coronado and bus candidates north to Camp Pendleton just to find clean surf. Defense advocates and local leaders are demanding immediate federal intervention, warning that our nation's most elite warfighters should never be compromised on home soil by a preventable cross-border environmental disaster.

Is it unacceptable that America's future Navy SEALs are being sickened by cross-border pollution during combat training? Sound off below.

A MIRACULOUS RECOVERY FOR A HERO

Incredible news out of Poland as Kraków hero police officer Artur Morański has officially been taken off the ventilator, regained consciousness, and is now breathing completely on his own.

Officer Morański was critically wounded in the line of duty during an active shooting, putting his life directly on the line to protect fleeing civilians and confront danger head-on.

Rushed to the hospital in critical condition and placed on life support, his fellow officers and citizens across the globe have been holding their breath and praying for his survival.

Doctors have now confirmed this massive milestone in his recovery, proving the relentless fighting spirit of this brave officer.

Drop a prayer and show your respect for Officer Morański and all law enforcement officers who put everything on the line to keep communities safe.

Sound off in the comments below, let’s send strength his way.

Follow @SRSClips for daily hero stories, law enforcement updates, and uncensored news.

U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has moved out of his private residence and relocated to a fortified military base following credible Iranian threats against his life.

As the public face and architect of Washington's aggressive economic pressure campaign against Tehran, including crushing sanctions and maritime enforcement, Bessent has become a primary target for foreign retaliation. Intelligence assessments indicate foreign plots targeting senior American officials remain an active national security priority.

How should Washington respond when foreign adversaries threaten Cabinet secretaries on American soil? Drop your thoughts in the comments below.

A POWERFUL MESSAGE FROM THE WHITE HOUSE

In an official statement shared with millions across the country, the White House delivered a clear and direct message reaffirming America’s spiritual foundation.

The statement declared that “The United States will always remain One Nation Under God,” reminding citizens of the words enshrined in the Pledge of Allegiance and rooted in the nation’s founding documents.

The declaration comes at a time when debates over tradition, faith in the public square, and national unity continue to shape cultural and political discussions across the country.

For millions of Americans, the affirmation serves as an inspiring reminder of the heritage and values that have guided the nation through its greatest trials and triumphs.

Do you believe standing firmly on “One Nation Under God” is vital to preserving America’s foundation and strength?

Drop an AMEN or share your thoughts below, let’s see where the community stands in the comments.

BREAKING NEWS FROM CAPITOL HILL

In a dramatic roll call vote on the House floor, lawmakers voted 211 to 204 to effectively block and kill an impeachment effort against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

The House approved a motion to refer the impeachment resolution to committee, shutting down an attempt to force a direct floor debate regarding Hegseth’s Caribbean counter-narcotics maritime strikes.

The vote largely followed party lines, with 210 Republicans voting to shield the Defense Secretary. Only one Republican broke ranks to vote against the motion, joining 203 Democrats.

Hegseth has vigorously defended the military operations, calling them lawful, constitutionally authorized, and vital to stopping the flow of deadly narcotics into American communities.

Where do you stand on the House vote to shut down this impeachment push? Was this the right call, or should there have been a full floor debate?

Drop your thoughts below, let’s see where the room stands in the comments.

SECOND AMENDMENT BATTLE IN TEXAS

On day one of prefiling for the upcoming Texas legislative session, state Democrats came out swinging with nearly 20 separate firearm bills aimed at overhauling Texas gun laws.

The newly filed measures push for red flag emergency protective orders, restrictions on semi-automatic firearms, raising the purchase age for certain rifles to 21, universal background checks, and mandatory waiting periods.

In a state known for permitless carry and strong Second Amendment protections backed by a conservative majority and Governor Greg Abbott, these proposals are setting off an immediate political showdown in Austin.

Proponents argue these measures represent common-sense steps to curb gun violence, while Second Amendment defenders argue they infringe directly on law-abiding citizens’ constitutional rights.

Where do you stand on these proposals? Do you believe any of these measures should pass, or should Texas hold the line on Second Amendment protections?

Sound off in the comments below, let’s see where the debate heads on this one.

Absolute chaos went down right in the middle of the streets of Chicago, and the footage is already spreading like wildfire across every platform.

A group of demonstrators literally pulled out an American flag, doused it, and set it completely ablaze right on the pavement—and it instantly triggered a vicious, screaming shouting match with furious bystanders and counter-protesters who rushed in.

Legally speaking, the Supreme Court has protected flag burning for decades under the First Amendment as a form of symbolic speech, meaning the act itself isn't a crime.

Culturally, and especially in the eyes of millions of veterans and citizens who respect the uniform, it's viewed as a brutal slap in the face and pure desecration of what people bled for overseas.

Local law enforcement had to roll in fast with specialized crowd-control units to build a literal wall between the two heated factions before full-scale punches and physical violence broke out.

It’s the same fierce, ongoing firestorm every single time—the ultimate clash where constitutional free expression slams head-first into deep national pride and respect.

A federal grand jury in Wichita, Kansas, has officially indicted a U.S. Postal Service worker after federal agents discovered thousands of pieces of undelivered mail hoarded inside her garage — including hundreds of election campaign mailers that were exclusively from the Republican Party.

According to court filings from the U.S. Attorney's Office, 59-year-old mail carrier Kelly R. Cram of Baxter Springs is facing federal charges for unlawful secretion, destruction, and delay of mail. Investigators with the USPS Office of Inspector General uncovered a staggering 4,404 pieces of mail intended for residents in and around Pittsburg, Kansas, stashed away in her home.

Among the recovered items, federal prosecutors confirmed that nearly 400 pieces were campaign mailers supporting Republican candidates and GOP political action committees. In contrast, federal agents found zero political mailers for Democrats or any other political party. Cram now faces federal prosecution as election integrity watchdogs demand strict accountability across mail delivery networks.

Do you believe incidents like this demand stricter federal oversight of election mail? Share your thoughts below.

The Battle of Ramadi, Iraq.

Ramadi was widely considered by military intelligence to be lost—a violent, insurgent-choked city dominated by al-Qaeda in Iraq where American patrols took fire on every street corner.

Into that meat grinder walked SEAL Team 3’s Task Unit Bruiser, commanded by Lieutenant Commander Jocko Willink.

Operating hand-in-hand with U.S. Army soldiers and Marines, Task Unit Bruiser established fortified outposts deep inside enemy territory, hunting insurgents night and day in brutal close-quarters combat.

Under Jocko’s command were some of the most decorated warriors in American history:

Michael Monsoor: Who threw his body onto a live grenade to save his teammates, earning the Medal of Honor.

Marc Lee: The first Navy SEAL to give his life in the Iraq War, fiercely firing into enemy positions to draw fire away from his brothers, earning the Silver Star.

Chris Kyle: The deadliest sniper in U.S. military history, earning two Silver Stars and five Bronze Stars with Valor.

Task Unit Bruiser became the most decorated Special Operations unit of the Iraq War.

But Jocko’s greatest leadership test came when a chaotic, high-stress fog-of-war engagement resulted in a fratricide incident. Instead of blaming junior troops, bad maps, or communication breakdowns, Jocko stood before his commanding officers and said four words that changed modern leadership forever:

"I am responsible. It's on me."

That battle-tested philosophy became Extreme Ownership—the principle that true leaders never make excuses, never blame external circumstances, and take absolute responsibility for everything in their world.

"Discipline equals freedom."

During a live stand-up comedy set at Madison Square Garden, legendary comedian Dave Chappelle stunned the arena when he addressed the murder of conservative activist Charlie Kirk—telling the audience that he actually "feels better" since Kirk's death.

While some in the crowd laughed, the remarks ignited immediate national backlash once audio of the set surfaced.

Charlie Kirk's widow, Erika Kirk, issued a blistering response, condemning high-profile commentators and comedians for treating political violence and the destruction of a human life as a punchline.

Here is the question that cuts to the core of modern culture: Have we become so politically polarized that the assassination of an ideological opponent is now considered acceptable material for arena comedy?

Dave Chappelle has long built his career on fearless, unfiltered comedy that challenges sacred cows across the political spectrum.

But there is a distinct line between pushing creative boundaries and celebrating the murder of a father and husband who was assassinated for his political beliefs. When cultural icons normalize violence for applause, it sends a dangerous signal through an already divided nation.

Did Dave Chappelle cross an unforgivable line with these remarks, or should stand-up comedians be granted total immunity on stage no matter how offensive the joke?

“UNDER ACTIVE SNIPER FIRE: HE DRAGGED HIS WOUNDED BROTHER THROUGH THE MUD TO SAFETY.”

On October 31, 2006, in the war-torn city of Karmah near Fallujah in Anbar Province, Iraq, a foot patrol from the 4th Mobile Assault Platoon (Weapons Company, 2nd Battalion, 8th Marines) was moving down a flooded, unpaved alleyway when a single gunshot broke the silence.

An insurgent sniper round struck 22-year-old Lance Corporal Juan Valdez-Castillo in the right arm, entered his chest, collapsed both lungs, ricocheted off a rib, and exited through his back, fracturing a vertebra.

Valdez-Castillo slammed into a cinderblock wall and collapsed into the freezing mud and standing water, suffocating and unable to move.

His squad leader, Sergeant Jesse E. Leach, didn't hesitate:

Sprinting into the Kill Zone: With the sniper still zeroed in on the alley, Sgt. Leach stepped directly into the open line of fire without waiting for suppressive coverage.

The Mud Drag: Grabbing the drag handle of Valdez-Castillo’s body armor with his left hand while keeping his M4 rifle aimed downrange with his right, Leach hauled his 200-pound teammate backward through thick, viscous canal mud toward the shelter of a concrete wall.

Capturing History: Embedded New York Times photojournalist Joao Silva and reporter C.J. Chivers captured the raw, straining rescue in real time, producing one of the most defining photographs of brotherhood in modern combat history.

Refusing to Quit: Behind cover, Leach applied emergency chest seals and stanched the catastrophic bleeding, stabilizing Valdez-Castillo until medevac forces arrived.

Sergeant Jesse Leach was awarded the Navy and Marine Corps Commendation Medal with Combat "V" for his valor under fire.

Against all odds, Juan Valdez-Castillo survived. After extensive surgeries and rehabilitation, he returned to Iraq, deployed to Afghanistan, retired as a sergeant, and later graduated from law school to spend his life advocating for wounded veterans.

“No Marine left behind is not a motto. It is an unbreakable promise written in blood and mud.”

“MY HELICOPTER CRASHED INTO BIN LADEN’S COMPOUND. AFTER EXTORTION 17, I WANTED TO DIE.” — SEAL Team 6 Operator Alex West on The Shawn Ryan Show.

In one of the most raw, heartbreaking conversations on The Shawn Ryan Show (Episode #114), former DEVGRU operator Alex West opened up about survivor’s guilt, post-traumatic stress, and the invisible scars of war.

After enlisting at 17 and becoming the youngest operator ever selected for SEAL Team 6, West survived 15 combat deployments—including the stealth Black Hawk crash during Operation Neptune Spear—only to lose his closest brothers three months later when callsign Extortion 17 was shot down in the Tangi Valley.

In his own words:

“I was in the tail of the helicopter when our bird lost lift and slammed into the courtyard wall inside Osama bin Laden’s compound in Abbottabad. The tail snapped, rotors chewed into the dirt, and we scrambled out directly into the assault.

We pulled off the biggest raid in modern history. But just three months later, Extortion 17 was shot down.

In a single second, 30 American service members—my entire squadron, the guys who stood next to me in Abbottabad, my mentors, my best friends—were completely incinerated in the Tangi Valley.

When that happened, my soul broke.

I went home and spiraled into pure darkness. I was drinking myself to death every single night just to make the screaming in my head stop. I would sit on the edge of my bed with a loaded pistol in my hand, staring at the floor, crying, begging for the courage to pull the trigger.

Surviving the raid that took out the world's most wanted terrorist meant nothing when all the men you loved were in body bags.”

Surviving the most dangerous missions on earth only to face your hardest battle alone in a dark room at home is a reality thousands of combat veterans know all too well.

Drop a salute in the comments for Alex West and the 30 warriors of Extortion 17 who never came home.

Long before he stood in the dust and smoke of Lower Manhattan, Rick Rescorla was already a legend of American military history — the young platoon leader pictured on the cover of We Were Soldiers Once… and Young who rallied his men through the savage 1965 Battle of Ia Drang.

Decades later, as head of corporate security for Morgan Stanley at the World Trade Center, Rescorla brought that same battle-tested discipline to civilian life. Following the 1993 truck bombing, he concluded that the towers remained vulnerable to an aerial attack and instituted mandatory, unannounced evacuation drills every few months. Executives grumbled about lost trading hours, but Rescorla was unyielding. He timed workers with a stopwatch, training thousands of employees to navigate dark stairwells until moving in an emergency became muscle memory.

On the morning of September 11, 2001, when American Airlines Flight 11 struck Tower One, building announcements blared over the PA system instructing workers in Tower Two to remain at their desks. Rescorla refused. Shouting into his bullhorn that everything above the impact zone was burning and that their building was in danger, he immediately ordered the complete evacuation of Morgan Stanley’s 22 floors.

As thousands of anxious workers descended the crowded stairwells, Rescorla walked beside them with his megaphone, singing Cornish marching songs and Welsh battle hymns to banish panic. Between choruses, he smiled and told his people to remain calm, proud, and steady. Over 2,600 Morgan Stanley employees made it out alive that morning.

After clearing his floors, Rescorla called his best friend Dan Hill from his mobile phone, stating calmly that the dumb bastards were telling him not to evacuate, but that he was getting his people out. When last seen alive on the tenth floor heading back up into the burning tower, colleagues urged him to leave. Rescorla shook his head and replied that as soon as he made sure everyone else was out, he would follow.

Moments later, Tower Two collapsed.

How does true leadership look when routine gives way to crisis?

#RickRescorla #NeverForget #TrueLeadership

PETE HEGSETH FACES IMPEACHMENT — 8 Articles Filed Over The Iran War, Boat Strikes, And The Maduro Raid. Do You Stand With Him?

A massive showdown is underway in Washington after Republican Representative Thomas Massie officially introduced eight articles of impeachment against Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth.

The resolution accuses Hegseth of constitutional and statutory violations, centering on the ongoing war in Iran, lethal strikes against suspected drug-running boats in the Caribbean, and the high-profile special operations raid that captured Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro.

Hegseth came out firing on Monday, waving off the impeachment push as "the politics of personal destruction" and standing firmly behind American warfighters, according to Al Jazeera —

"If you want to take issue with what we did in Epic Fury or Rough Rider or nabbing Nicolás Maduro, you're taking issue with the troops and what they accomplished, which is historic." — Pete Hegseth

President Trump has backed his defense secretary 100%, praising Hegseth's wartime leadership while House lawmakers prepare for a high-stakes floor debate later this week.

For decades, the most ironic part of joining the world’s premier air service was that recruits could spend their entire time in boot camp without ever laying eyes on an actual military aircraft. Outside of the commercial flight bringing them into San Antonio, the standard experience at Basic Military Training was virtually indistinguishable from other service branches, revolving around endless hours of ceremonial marching, precision bed-making, locker inspections, and rulebook memorization.

Now, the service is fundamentally transforming boot camp through its BMT Next initiative at Joint Base San Antonio-Lackland in Texas.
Instead of spending weeks drilling on the parade grounds, incoming airmen are stepping directly onto simulated operational airfields centered around retired, full-scale combat airframes, including F-16 Fighting Falcons and C-130 Hercules transports. The objective is to rewire recruit training around practical warfighting and the Pentagon’s Agile Combat Employment doctrine, which expects airmen of every career specialty to help generate combat sorties from austere, dispersed forward bases under hostile conditions.

Throughout the revamped curriculum and its culminating PACER FORGE deployment exercise, recruits train in high-tempo, hands-on tasks that mimic real airfield threats. Trainees practice rapid runway crater repair, expeditionary refueling operations, weapons loading, aircraft marshaling, casualty evacuation, and forward perimeter defense against simulated ground assaults. The program even incorporates analog map-and-compass navigation drills to ensure future airmen can coordinate operations across a chaotic flightline when GPS signals and digital communications are jammed or destroyed by an adversary.

By cutting back on legacy ceremonial drill and shifting the curriculum to real airframes, the Air Force aims to instill operational discipline and an expeditionary mindset from day one of enlistment.

Does shifting boot camp from ceremonial military traditions to hands-on combat tasks better prepare the next generation of troops for modern warfare?

Already shot through both legs during a brutal courtyard firefight in Paktia Province, Afghanistan, Army Ranger SFC Leroy Petry refused to leave his two wounded teammates behind.

When a live enemy grenade landed just feet from where they were pinned down, Petry didn't hesitate. With no regard for his own life, he lunged forward, seized the armed grenade with his bare right hand, and hurled it away from his brothers.

The grenade detonated as it left his grip, severing his hand and peppering him with shrapnel, but his decisive gallantry completely shielded his teammates from the blast. For his extraordinary valor and selflessness, Sergeant First Class Leroy Petry was awarded the Medal of Honor.

Share this post to honor SFC Leroy Petry and the warriors of the 75th Ranger Regiment who put everything on the line for their brothers.

The Army is halting future buys of its brand-new M7 service rifle after ordering nearly 15,000 lighter M8 carbines.

In one of the fastest design corrections in modern small-arms history, the Pentagon’s latest budget request seeks 14,944 new M8 carbines while zeroing out any future purchases of the full-sized M7 rifle. Despite already taking delivery of roughly 50,000 M7s, frontline infantrymen and test units quickly sounded the alarm that the 13-inch rifle was simply too heavy, front-heavy, and cumbersome to maneuver in close-quarters combat once paired with its mandatory suppressor and computerized M157 smart optic.

Now, gunmaker SIG Sauer has revealed they saw the backlash coming before the military even signed the contract. Company executives explained that rigid initial Pentagon specifications originally forced them to build the bulkier M7 design. Anticipating soldier frustration, SIG engineers proactively developed the shorter, 10.4-inch barrel M8 carbine on their own initiative so an answer was waiting the moment the Army asked for it.

The resulting M8 is over a full pound lighter, 3.5 inches shorter, ditches the folding stock for a rigid setup, and runs 25-round magazines without sacrificing the devastating terminal ballistics of the new 6.8x51mm cartridge. Initial operational fielding begins next month at Fort Bragg.

Does quickly adopting the compact M8 prove that the military is finally listening to real soldier feedback, or does ditching the M7 so soon expose another multi-million dollar Pentagon procurement blunder?

Drop your thoughts below.

#USArmy #M8Carbine #SigSauer

BLUE ANGELS SCANDAL  Pilot Booted From Elite Squadron, Now The Officer He Mentored Has Also Disappeared. What Really Happened?

A growing mystery is sweeping through naval aviation after the U.S. Navy abruptly removed Marine Corps Major Scott Laux, the Blue Angels No. 6 opposing solo pilot, ahead of their homecoming airshow in Pensacola, Florida, as reported by Newsweek.

Officials stated only that Laux "failed to uphold standards," forcing the demonstration team to fly with five jets instead of their signature six-jet formation.

Netizens and military observers quickly noticed that Marine Captain Danielle Cribb, the squadron's Public Affairs Officer whom Laux openly mentored, was also quietly scrubbed from the Blue Angels official website and team roster without any public explanation, according to reporting from The Aviationist and SFGATE.

Key details confirmed so far —

 Major Scott Laux was dismissed immediately prior to the season-ending airshow with no official misconduct charges publicly disclosed.

Captain Danielle Cribb, who joined the Blue Angels in 2025 and listed Laux as her mentor, was removed from the squadron roster around the same timeframe.

Naval Air Training officials have declined to specify whether the dual departures stem from flight safety violations, professional friction, or personal policy issues.

Do you think the Navy owes the public a full explanation, or should internal squadron matters stay behind closed doors?

A massive national debate has erupted after newly elected Michigan Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed declared Michigan the "capital of Arab America" during a speech in Washington, D.C.

Turning Point USA CEO Erika Kirk fired back immediately with a response that is setting the internet on fire —

The controversy centers on two opposing views of the country —

Abdul El-Sayed celebrated his historic Senate victory by calling his home state the heart of Arab America.

 Erika Kirk argued that dividing the country into separate cultural sub-nations undermines unity under one American flag.

 Supporters on both sides are clashing across every social platform in one of the most heated debates of the year.

Did she say what needed to be said, or was she out of line?

Sgt Daniel Gurr
Died: August 5, 2011

21, of Vernal, Utah; assigned to 3rd Reconnaissance Battalion, 3rd Marine Division, II Marine Expeditionary Force (Forward), Okinawa, Japan; died Aug. 5 in Helmand province, Afghanistan, while conducting combat operations.

From The Vernal Express 8/9/2011

Sgt. Daniel David Gurr USMC was taken back to the loving arms of his Heavenly Father on Aug. 5, 2011. He was killed while defending his country in Afghanistan.

Daniel was born March 17, 1990 to David and Tracy Gurr. He was the second of four children. Daniel graduated from Uintah High School in 2008 where served as a member of his Junior Class Presidency. He participated in football, was the captain of his soccer team and was named as an All American. During his senior year he joined the Marine Corps which had been his lifelong ambition.

Daniel was full of life! His smile would brighten any room that he walked into, he brought joy to everyone he met. Anything that he did was done with all the energy and enthusiasm he had. Daniel enjoyed doing most anything, camping, hunting, fishing, riding four-wheelers and snowboarding, but most of all he enjoyed stirring up excitement while hanging out with family and friends.

Daniel had always wanted to be a Marine. He wanted to be the best and poured his heart and soul into his career. His great-grandfather AA (Mac) McCarrel was a veteran of World War II who had fought in the South Pacific was Daniel’s hero and Daniel was Mac’s. He was very proud of him. Daniel is and always will be our hero! He will greatly missed by all who knew him.

Daniel is survived by his mother, Tracy Beede; father, David (Dana) Gurr; sisters, Ashley (Shane) Mecham and Caitlyn Gurr; brother, Austin Gurr; and nephew, Karsyn Gurr; numerous step brothers and step sister; maternal grandparents, Georgia and Mike Vander Linden (Vernal); Dean and Connie Abplanalp (Florida); paternal grandparents, Gen and Janet Gurr (Vernal); many great-grandparents; aunts; uncles and cousins; his high school sweetheart Stephanie Sabin; and his Marine brothers in 3rd Reconnaissance Battalion, 3rd Marine Division. Daniel was preceded in death by his great grandparents AA (Mac) and Adoree McCarrel and great-grandfather Earl Gurr.

FLORIDA LEARJET DISASTER  NTSB Recovers Cockpit Voice Recorder From Deep Crater. Will The Audio Reveal What Happened?

Federal investigators with the NTSB have officially recovered the cockpit voice recorder from the Learjet 60 that crashed near Greenacres, Florida, claiming the lives of all nine people on board.

The heavily damaged orange recorder was unearthed from the impact crater and immediately flown to the agency's specialized Vehicle Recorders Laboratory in Washington, D.C., where audio engineers are working to extract the final minutes of crew conversations.

Key investigation updates confirmed by federal officials —

Excavation Completed — Search crews have wrapped up excavation work at the primary impact crater near Greenacres after recovering the flight recorder and engine components reported by CNN.

Crucial Audio Evidence — Specialized engineers in Washington, D.C. are evaluating whether the battered unit's memory modules survived the extreme impact to provide cockpit communications and flight deck warnings.

Debris Field Clues — Investigators previously documented that parts of the jet's left elevator separated in flight between 1.3 and 3.8 miles before the aircraft entered its fatal vertical descent, according to tracking data on Flightradar24.

What do you think caused this catastrophic descent — mechanical failure, severe turbulence, or an in-flight breakup?

The U.S. Army has officially given its culinary specialists a battlefield rebrand, formally redesignating soldiers holding the 92G military occupational specialty as “tactical field feeding specialists.”

The title change was officially approved by Headquarters, Department of the Army G-1 and unveiled during a redesignation ceremony hosted by the Quartermaster School at Fort Gregg-Adams.

The Army first established food service specialists under the 94B identifier in the 1960s before transitioning the MOS to 92G Culinary Specialist in 1995. Now, service leaders say the latest rebrand reflects a strategic shift away from routine garrison dining facilities toward large-scale combat operations in austere, contested environments.

With the military increasingly privatizing installation dining facilities, 92Gs are being realigned toward mobile kitchen trailers, assault feeding systems, and expeditionary containerized kitchens designed to sustain troops on dispersed frontlines.

Naturally, the grandiose new job title has sparked endless humor across the ranks, with troops joking about high-speed combat spatulas, tactical ladle deployments, and operator-grade scrambled eggs.

Yet Army leadership stands by the change, emphasizing that sustained frontline combat power requires agile logistical feeding capable of operating under fire.

Does rebranding Army cooks as tactical field feeders reflect genuine battlefield modernization, or is it classic military bureaucracy at work?

#USArmy #MilitaryLife #92G

Under the Justice for Citizens Wrongfully Detained by ICE Act, introduced in Congress by Representative Teresa Leger Fernández, U.S. citizens who are unlawfully arrested or detained by federal immigration officers without a warrant or probable cause would receive an express right to sue in federal court. If successful, the legislation mandates a minimum statutory payout of $500,000 for the initial detention, with an additional $100,000 awarded for every subsequent day spent behind bars. Crucially, the bill strips officers of qualified immunity and waives the federal government’s sovereign immunity defenses, removing the legal shield that historically derailed wrongful arrest lawsuits.

The legislative push follows a wave of high-profile incidents and investigative reports, including findings cited by Newsweek revealing that more than 500 American citizens have been stopped, questioned, or held at gunpoint during aggressive immigration operations since early 2025. Civil rights organizations and groups like LULAC argue that without severe financial penalties, federal paramilitaries will continue operating on a "grab first, justify later" mentality that routinely violates Fourth Amendment protections based on skin tone and language.

The Department of Homeland Security and conservative lawmakers have mounted fierce opposition, warning that six-figure automatic bounties would undermine frontline law enforcement, expose agents to personal legal harassment, and incentivize political activists to deliberately obstruct lawful enforcement sweeps against dangerous criminal aliens.

Should taxpayers automatically pay six-figure damages to citizens caught in immigration sweeps to deter federal overreach, or does stripping officer immunity handcuff agents tasked with securing the homeland?

Marine Staff Sgt. Patrick R. Dolphin
Died July 31, 2011 Serving During Operation Enduring Freedom

CAMP LEATHERNECK, Afghanistan (Oct. 3, 2010) - As bullets whizzed past, Gunnery Sgt. Eric J. Fears knew one thing; he had to continue with the mission even though two of his Marines had just been killed by an improvised explosive device. He showed his Marines that they had to keep fighting, and they did. 

On Oct. 3, Fears was presented with a Bronze Star Medal with Combat Distinguishing Device for his heroic actions on that day in Jan. 2009 as a squad leader with 3d Battalion, 8th Marine Regiment in support of Operation Enduring Freedom.

After the deadly IED attack, Fears managed to stay calm and focused despite being under heavy small arms fire and indirect fire from an entrenched enemy. The mission at hand and recovering the bodies of his two men became his focus.

“Two of my Marines were hit with an IED,” said Fears, now the staff non-commissioned officer in charge of Bridge Platoon, Alpha Company, 9th Engineer Support Battalion, 1st Marine Logistics Group (Forward). “We were taking a lot of fire, but we made sure to get them back.”

Fears encouraged his Marines to keep fighting even though they lost two of their own. Through his courage, he set the example for his Marines.
“On that day, he showed his Marines it takes good leadership and a lot of courage to continue on with the mission,” said First Sgt. Lawrence D. Wei, the Alpha Co. first sergeant with 9th ESB, 1st MLG (FWD).

Fears is a strong leader who adds a great amount of skill to the Marines of 9th ESB through his vast experience and knowledge.

“He's experienced,” said Wei. “He has had seven deployments, and he has been in division and now he's in MLG. You don't really find all the qualifications he has in everyone.”

Fears' solid character, which makes him successful in the Marine Corps, does not go unnoticed by those he serves under.

“He's very calm, patient and firm,” said Wei. “Everything that makes him a good Marine was required of him that day.”

Fears accepted the award, but passed the credit to his Marines.

“I'm honored, very honored,” said Fears from Blue Ridge, Ga., “I earned this for when I was attached to 3/8, and my Marines were on the front lines and were finding a lot of IEDs. I wear this Bronze Star not just for myself, but all the engineers that were with me at the time.”

Part of the Soldier’s Creed is never to leave behind a fallen comrade. On the night of March 13, 2006, then-Sgt. Wilzcek, Sgt. Row, then-Pfc. Alvarez, then-Pfc. Pushkin and the rest of their squad risked life and limb to live up to that promise.

Row, the point man, was leading the soldiers through dark, narrow alleys in the city of Ramadi as the squad headed back to base. Suddenly, two men darted into a nearby house, and at that hour, Row saw that as a clear sign of imminent danger. He stopped the team, but within seconds the street exploded with an onslaught of machine-gun and small-arms fire, RPG explosions, and hand grenades. The squad dropped to the ground and directed fire at the enemy’s position.

Alvarez moved to a covered position to reload his weapon, and he noticed one of his comrades had been hit and was lying in the middle of the firefight. Without hesitation, Alvarez rushed into the kill zone to check the soldier’s vital signs – but it was too late. He covered the soldier’s body with his own and continued firing on the enemy. When he ran out of ammunition, Alvarez stood up and started dragging the soldier out of the line of fire. Row, who was pinned down nearby, provided cover fire as Alvarez struggled to move the body. When Wilzcek and Pushkin saw Alvarez’s difficulties, they ran into the open to help. But as the three moved back toward cover, two RPGs exploded 10 meters away, knocking them down and sending a volley of shrapnel into Alvarez’s right knee. The men stood up and continued dragging their comrade to the safety of a nearby courtyard.

After establishing a safe area for the injured, Pushkin and Wilzcek ran back and forth several times from the courtyard into the line of fire to rescue trapped soldiers. Meanwhile, the RPG explosions had also injured Row’s elbow with shrapnel. Even so, he continued firing on the enemy position to help the others reach safety. Once everyone was clear, Row, who was alone in the middle of the street, called for help. As Row remembered later, “I was trapped in the street, and [Pushkin and Wilzcek] pulled me out of there.”

The squad was now in the courtyard, and medical assistance was being administered – but their work was not done: enemy fire continued to light up the area. When the squad started planning the next phase, Alvarez refused to be moved with the other injured soldiers, staying to help in the fight.

The insurgents, seeing the evacuation in progress, focused their fire on the rescuers. Wilzcek, already on the roof, began firing back. After clearing the rooms below, Pushkin and his team hurried up to the roof to help Wilzcek. Row grabbed a Bunker Defeat Munition – a shoulder-launched explosive for use against fortified positions – but his injured elbow prevented him from using it. He ran up to the roof, handed the weapon to Pushkin, and helped guide Pushkin toward the targets. With Row and Wilzcek providing cover fire, Pushkin took aim and fired, destroying the enemy’s position and killing a number of insurgents. With that, the squad was able to leave the area safely.

3,800 meters. 2.36 miles. 12,467 feet.

A bullet took nearly nine full seconds in flight before striking its target—shattering the confirmed world record for the longest sniper kill in human history.

The shot was made by 58-year-old Ukrainian SBU counter-intelligence sniper Viacheslav Kovalskyi and his spotter across the Dnipro River in the Kherson region.

At a distance of over 41 football fields, hitting a human-sized target defies conventional ballistic physics:

The Coriolis Effect: Because the bullet stayed airborne for nearly nine seconds, the sniper team had to calculate the physical rotation of the Earth beneath the projectile.

Massive Bullet Drop: The bullet dropped over 300 feet (100+ meters) from apex to impact, requiring the shooter to angle the rifle high into the sky like an artillery piece.

Shifting Winds: Factoring in temperature, barometric air pressure, humidity, and varying crosswinds across two miles of open water and terrain.

The hardware behind the shot was just as extreme: the custom "Horizon's Lord" (Volodar Obriyu) anti-materiel precision rifle, measuring over six feet in length.

In the bottom of the photo, you can see why this rifle reaches where standard weapons fail:

On the right is a standard .50 BMG (12.7x99mm) round.

On the left is the monster 12.7x114mm HL cartridge—a massive 14.5mm anti-aircraft casing necked down to fire a heavy .50-caliber precision match bullet at over 3,400 feet per second, keeping the projectile supersonic far past two miles.

The shot surpassed the previous world record held by a Canadian JTF-2 sniper in Iraq (3,540 meters) and pushed the outer limits of extreme long-range shooting.

To our long-range shooters and snipers: factoring in a 9-second flight time, the Coriolis effect, and crosswinds across 2.36 miles—how much of this shot was pure mathematical mastery, and how much was divine luck?

“IF YOU ARE COMING IN HERE WITH SORROW, GO ELSEWHERE. I AM GOING TO MAKE A FULL RECOVERY.” — Navy SEAL Jason Redman on The Shawn Ryan Show.

In one of the most inspirational conversations in the history of The Shawn Ryan Show (Episode #032), wounded Navy SEAL Lieutenant Jason Redman recounted the 2007 ambush outside Fallujah where he was struck by eight rounds including heavy machine-gun fire that shattered his arm and tore away half his face and the legendary sign he taped to his hospital door.

In his own words:

“When I woke up at Bethesda, my face was rebuilt with metal plates, my jaw was wired shut, and my arm was completely shredded.

People would walk into my hospital room family members, friends, senior officers and the moment they looked at me, their faces would melt into pure horror and grief. They would start crying, sobbing, looking at me with this sickening pity, as if my life was completely over.

That look made me sick to my stomach. I was alive. My guys were alive.

I grabbed a bright orange poster board and a black Sharpie, and with my one good hand, I wrote a sign and taped it directly to the front door of my hospital room:

 If you are coming into this room with sorrow or to feel sorry for my wounds, go elsewhere. The wounds I received I got in a job I love, doing it for people I love, supporting the freedom of a country I deeply love. I am incredibly tough and will make a full recovery. If you are not prepared for that, go elsewhere. But if you are, welcome to my room.’

That sign became our line in the sand. You don’t get to mourn me while I’m still standing.”

Jason Redman endured 37 surgeries, extensive facial reconstruction, and years of physical therapy, going on to write The Trident and Overcome and dedicating his life to helping combat veterans conquer their own life ambushes.

Banning pity from your hospital room while your jaw is wired shut and your face is held together with titanium plates is the ultimate definition of the warrior mindset.

When Senator Joe Biden held up a TEC-9 during a Senate Judiciary Committee hearing on assault weapons.

In August 1993, then-Senator Joe Biden created one of the most famous visual moments in congressional gun control history when he raised a black Intratec TEC-9 semi-automatic pistol above the dais in the Senate Judiciary Committee.

The story behind the iconic hearing:

• The Catalyst: The hearing took place in the immediate aftermath of the July 1993 mass shooting at 101 California Street in San Francisco, where a gunman armed with modified TEC-9 pistols killed eight people.

• The Demonstration: As Chairman of the Senate Judiciary Committee, Biden held up the firearm during testimony to argue that weapons with military-style features—such as barrel shrouds, threaded barrels, and high-capacity magazines—served no legitimate sporting or hunting purpose.

• The Legislative Legacy: That hearing provided the critical political momentum for the landmark 1994 Federal Assault Weapons Ban, passed as part of the 1994 Crime Bill, which banned the TEC-9 by name alongside 18 other models and restricted civilian magazines over 10 rounds for a decade before sunsetting in 2004.

More than three decades later, this image remains one of the defining symbols of the modern Second Amendment debate on Capitol Hill.

Lance Corporal Thomas Adametz secured a Fallujah house with his platoon. Suddenly, an insurgent force between 50 and 100 strong ambushed their position with grenades, RPGs, and automatic weapons. On the rooftop, numerous Marines were wounded, 4 seriously. One Marine went down, dropping his Squad Automatic Weapon. LCpl Adametz took over the machine gun and went to work. Completely exposed, Adametz laid down suppressive fire, driving back the enemy now just yards away from the Marines' building and allowing the evacuation of the wounded. When the barrel of his SAW warped and overheated, Adametz severely burned his hand, removing it. He ignored the burns, inserted a new barrel, and continued firing. His actions allowed the successful medevacs and played a key role in preventing their position from being overrun. For his heroic initiative and courage, Adametz was awarded the Silver Star.

"...serving as a Rifleman, Echo Company, Second Battalion, First Marines, on 26 April 2004. Following the seizure of two key buildings along a vital avenue of approach into the company's sector, LCpl Adametz and his squad moved into the northernmost building and provided security for his platoon's position. The enemy's fierce attack of RPGs and hand grenades on his platoon's position resulted in four serious and numerous minor casualties. With disregard for his own safety, LCpl Adametz exposed himself to grenades and small arms fire in order to provide suppressive fire, facilitating the evacuation of the wounded Marines. Picking up a SAW from a wounded Marine, he delivered withering fire on enemy forces 25 meters away. LCpl Adametz' aggressive actions and devastating fire were critical in repelling the enemy's attack."

On the left is what internet culture thinks a dangerous operator looks like: full sleeves, a thick beard, tactical gear, and a scowl.

On the right is what actual lethality looks like: a quiet, mild-mannered man with wire-rimmed glasses who looks like an accountant—Sergeant Major Mike Vining (U.S. Army, Ret.).

Don't let the smile fool you. Mike Vining is one of the most lethal, decorated, and revered warriors in the history of American Special Operations.

Look closely at the uniform:

Combat Infantryman Badge (CIB)

Master Explosive Ordnance Disposal (EOD) Badge

Master Parachutist Badge with Combat Jump Star

Military Free Fall (HALO) Parachutist Badge

Legion of Merit & Bronze Star Medal

Drafted in 1968, Vining served in Vietnam disarming booby traps, unexploded ordnance, and clearing enemy tunnel complexes under fire.

In 1978, when Colonel Charles Beckwith created 1st SFOD-D (Delta Force) to be America's premier counter-terrorist unit, Mike Vining answered the call. He passed the inaugural selection course and became a founding operator of Delta Force.

Over his career, SGM Vining served on the frontlines of history:

Operation Eagle Claw (1980): Part of the Delta assault force in the Iranian desert.

Operation Urgent Fury (1983): Assaulted the Richmond Hill prison in Grenada, surviving an anti-aircraft shootdown into the sea.

Operation Desert Storm (1991): Hunting Scud missile launchers deep behind enemy lines in Iraq.

The loudest men in the room are rarely the most dangerous.

The truly lethal ones are the quiet professionals who never brag, never posture, and carry decades of silent master craftsmanship in their trade.

Never judge a warrior by his appearance.

In the spring of 2002, Pat Tillman had the world at his feet.

At twenty-five years old, he had defied the odds as a seventh-round draft pick to become a starting safety for the Arizona Cardinals, breaking franchise tackle records and earning the respect of players across the NFL. The team placed a three-year, 3.6 million dollar contract extension on the table.

Then came the morning of September 11, 2001.

Deeply shaken by the attacks on America, Tillman looked around at his life and decided that some things were bigger than football, fame, or financial security. In May 2002, without seeking publicity or fanfare, he turned down the multi-million dollar contract and walked into an Army recruiting station alongside his younger brother Kevin.

The two brothers volunteered for the infantry, completed airborne training, and earned their tan berets in the elite 2nd Battalion, 75th Ranger Regiment.

Tillman deployed to Iraq during the opening invasion in 2003, returned stateside to graduate from Ranger School, and deployed again to eastern Afghanistan in early 2004. On April 22, 2004, while maneuvering aggressively toward enemy positions during a chaotic ambush in Khost Province, Corporal Tillman was tragically killed in a friendly fire incident.

He never asked for a spotlight, refused all media interviews while in uniform, and simply wanted to serve alongside his fellow soldiers as an equal.

Pat Tillman gave up everything the world tells men to chase so that he could stand on the line for his country.

Rangers Lead the Way.

Capt. Brian Erickson, a pilot from the 75th Fighter Squadron, was awarded the Distinguished Flying Cross with Valor on July 11, 2008.

Capt. Brian Erickson, 75th FS chief of mission planning, earned the medal while deployed to Bagram Air Base, Afghanistan, for providing ground alert close air support to a German Provincial Reconstruction Team that was under nighttime fire from insurgents in a valley of the Hindu-Kush mountains.

"I'm extremely impressed with the way Captain Erickson handled himself out there," said Colonel Kenneth Todorov, 23rd Wing commander, "He provided close air support in hazardous conditions, with no forward air controller and led a successful mission with valor."

On Oct. 16, 2006, Captain Erickson and his wingman, who were then part of the 75th Expeditionary Fighter Squadron, received a short-notice call to provide aerial support to six German soldiers trapped between two mountain ranges. They were receiving enemy fire in the form of rocket-propelled grenades, machine guns, and small-arms fire.

Up until the call, previous flights of non-tactical aircraft had been unable to help the stranded PRT due to their location, limited communication capabilities, and lack of moonlight. Without illumination from the moon or another source, the pilots' night vision goggles provided little assistance.

Once he arrived on scene, Captain Erickson determined there was room for only one aircraft above the mountain tops and just below the clouds. He assigned the safe altitude above the clouds to his wingman, who searched for the insurgents' location with his advanced targeting pod and night vision goggles.

As Captain Erickson flew his A-10 deep into the moonless valley, where the only light on the ground was from insurgent weapons fire, his wingman flew above to relay reports about where the weapon bursts were coming from. Before Capt. Erickson could employ any of his own weapons, he needed to determine the exact location of the PRT to avoid friendly fire.

"I initially had my infrared sensor on to pinpoint the location of the insurgents. The problem with using the infrared was that every time a rocket-propelled grenade went off, the glow impeded my ability to navigate the dark canyon. The whole screen would go white, and I couldn't see outside my cockpit. The only solution was to turn the screens off," said Captain Erickson.

After Captain Erickson turned off his infrared sensor, he continued his low-level runs in search of the PRT. This proved an even more difficult task because the PRT's signaling device, an infrared strobe, was malfunctioning, and the German soldiers, who were untrained in communicating with aircraft, continued to take harassing enemy fire. The chaos of the situation was impaired even more by the PRT's limited proficiency in English. These limitations in combination with the enemy fire caused the PRT to provide confusing information on their exact location.

Realizing that time was running out for the PRT, Captain Erickson released a series of covert illumination flares only visible through night vision devices. Able to "see", he used geographic references from the air and ground to narrow down the PRT's location. During this time, the captain and his wingman were able to identify a location where they believed the enemy fire was coming from.

To be sure of the PRT's location, Captain Erickson conducted a low-altitude show-of-force. He flew between the enemy and friendly positions at 2,000 feet and deployed pyrotechnic self-protection flares, which lit the night sky. His hope was that the enemy would alert to his position and break their attack on the PRT long enough for his wingman to search for clues of the enemy's exact position.

"After we located where we thought the insurgents were, I had my wingman light-up the area with his targeting pod," said Captain Erickson. "During this time the weapons-fire against the Germans was also becoming increasingly accurate, and the need to bring the situation to a close was becoming more-and-more imperative. After we were able to determine that we were, in fact, targeting the insurgents and not the pinned-down German PRT team, it was time to take action."

With Captain Erickson's wingman marking the enemy's position with his TGP's infrared pointer, the PRT confirmed the mark as the enemy fire point of origin. In a single pass, Captain Erickson employed 240 30-millimeter rounds from the aircraft's GAU-8 cannon. This completely halted the enemy's fire and saved the lives of six German soldiers.

Captain Erickson and his wingman remained in the area to monitor both the friendly and enemy positions until the Iraqi National Police and International Security Assistance Force Quick Reaction Force were able to reach and recover the PRT and bring them to safety.

Captain Erickson credited the operation's success to his training. Although he was honored to receive the Distinguished Flying Cross with Valor for "doing the job he's trained to do," he pointed out a higher honor.

"The real reward was returning those six coalition soldiers safely to the village they were working at as part of the PRT team," said Captain Erickson.

Margaret Bourke-White was already the most famous photographer in America when she talked her way into the Pacific war. LIFE magazine's star shooter flew on bombing missions, dodged flak, and photographed the war in the Pacific so the folks back home could see it.

She was the first woman accredited as a war correspondent, and she earned it the hard way — in the air over enemy territory with a camera instead of a gun. Her images defined how America remembers the war.
